title: Choosing your first carving wood
subtitle: How to read the species, state, and grain before you pick up a knife
excerpt: The most common reason a first project fails is the wrong timber. This guide covers the five species that suit beginners, how to read green versus seasoned for the project in hand, what the grain tells you before the first cut, and where to source a first billet without spending much.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885) for the species comparison; Newey & Drage Practical Carpentry for the moisture-state and grain-reading framework.

glossaryTerms.definition: Freshly felled or recently riven wood, still high in moisture content. Carves much more easily than seasoned timber under a hand knife.
A short length of split or round timber, ready to be worked.
A short straight-bladed knife with a stout handle; the right starting knife for all the projects in this sub-category.

content.text: Timber matters more than technique at the start. This guide covers five beginner species, green versus seasoned wood, grain reading, and finding a cheap first billet.
The five beginner species
There is no universal best carving wood, but there is a short list of species that suit beginners across the projects in this sub-category.
Lime (Tilia europaea)

The sculptor's standard. Lime cuts cleanly in any grain direction, has almost no hard-soft ring contrast, and gives crisp fine detail under a detail knife. It is the best wood for small faces, relief carving, and chip carving. Availability: lime-avenue prunings from parks and councils; lime-coppice from craft suppliers. Food-safe under raw linseed oil.
Hazel (Corylus avellana)
The best source of green-wood
billets

in the UK and Europe. Coppice hazel produces straight rods; the wood is even-grained and carves well in the green state. It checks slightly as it dries, which is why the carving is done green and the piece is allowed to dry slowly in the finished shape. Food-safe under raw linseed oil.
Sycamore (Acer pseudoplatanus)
The traditional dairy and food-use timber. Pale and close-grained, food-safe. Harder than lime or hazel, but not difficult with a sharp
sloyd knife
. Better in the seasoned state for kitchen pieces because it is less prone to checking after drying.
Birch (Betula pendula)

Pale, fine-grained, and available from most woodland. Birch is the traditional kuksa timber in Scandinavia and a good all-round carving wood for green work. It is slightly harder than lime but softer than sycamore. Birch from young branches has a soft pith that pushes out cleanly for the whistle project.
Cherry (Prunus avium)

Harder than the four above, but takes a finer finished edge than any of them. Cherry darkens with age to a warm red-brown, which makes it the best choice for small decorative pieces. Pruning off-cuts from orchards and gardens are the main source. Cherry is food-safe under raw linseed oil. Carve green for the easiest work.
Green versus seasoned: what the project needs
The choice between
green wood

and seasoned is not a preference, it is a design decision. Green wood carves much more easily but shrinks and may check slightly as it dries. Seasoned wood is stable once worked but resists the knife more.
Use green wood for carved pieces such as spoons and kuksa blanks, and any work where slight shrinkage during drying is fine. The carving is much easier.
Use seasoned wood for: boxes, frames, salt scoops, and any piece with cut joinery that must stay dimensionally stable. Harder to carve but no drying movement.
How to tell green from seasoned without a meter

A freshly cut billet: the cut end darkens within seconds (the sap oxidises), and chips from a knife cut fly cleanly and feel cool. A seasoned piece: the end-grain is dull and dry; a knife chip crumbles rather than flies clean; the weight is noticeably less than a green billet of the same size.
Reading the grain before the first cut

On the side of any billet, the grain lines run from end to end. If they run perfectly parallel to the long axis, cuts along that axis go cleanly in both directions. If the grain slopes away to one side, the wood is easier to cut in the direction it slopes toward, cutting the other way goes against the grain and the surface tears or lifts. Hold the billet up to a light and sight along the cut surface after the first push cut: the surface should be smooth and slightly glossy if you are going with the grain; rough and lifted if you are going against it. Change direction if the surface is rough.
Where to source a first billet
Local tree surgeons: the best free source. Ring ahead and ask to be called when they are working on hazel, lime, cherry, or sycamore. Green billets stored in water keep usable for one to two weeks.
Coppice woodlands: most coppice operations sell small quantities of fresh rods. The Bodgers Association and the Coppice Association North West are starting points.
Online craft-wood suppliers: kiln-dried lime blocks in small sizes are available for around a few pounds. Good for first carved faces and relief work.
Example project: hazel spoon

A hazel jam spoon from a freshly cut coppice rod is the best first project. The billet is free or cheap, it carves almost without resistance, and the grain is straight enough that grain-reading is not yet critical. After one spoon, the second choice of timber is informed by experience rather than theory.
